newsitem.title: GERMANY: INSTANT VIEW - Comments on Bonn/Buba compromise.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Comments on Bonn/Buba compromise.

text.p: The German government said on Tuesday it had struck a compromise deal with the Bundesbank which would allow a payout of money from a revaluation of Bundesbank assets next year.

Bonn had originally hoped to gain a transfer this year from the revaluation which would have helped to reduce its debt and thus its interest rate payments in the key year for qualification for Eureopean monetary union.
Analysts made the following comments in a reaction to the agreement.
STEFAN SCHNEIDER, BANQUE PARIBAS in Frankfurt

Asked how Bonn can now hope to stop its deficit gaps and meet the Maastricht deficit targets: "That's a very tricky issue. I think the outcome of the clash (between the CDU and FDP on whether to raise indirect taxes) will be decisive. The liberals may have to cave in as otherwise the CDU may turn to the SPD for compromise. If there is a split in the government the liberals will be the losers.

Asked on the timing of the transfer, given that the revaluation is due to take effect in stages from 1997: "The revaluation is one thing, the actual profit transfer is another, stick with the fine print. The question is when the revaluation profits will be transfered."

On the French government's expressed wish to negotiate the stability pact: "The Maastricht Treaty is already signed and sealed so the targets set. But stability pact is different as they only have a comprehensive draft...But I believe that it will not be renegotiated and that they (the French) will find they can live with the stability pact."
On chances for Italy now being in EMU: "There was a chance that Italy would be out, but given Jospin's urge for a wider EMU, the chances that Italy will be in at the beginning are about 50 percent."
"Question now is how will conversations take place between the French socialists and the German government.
On the bond market outlook: "The market has reacted late to the fact that the government has backed down. I think the market fear over the longer time will be that we will get a soft euro."

KEITH EDMONDS, SENIOR ECONOMIST AT IBJ INTERNATIONAL: "The political driving force behind EMU is very great. Politicians will do anything to avoid delay. Nonetheless the chance of delay is now quite great.
The French election and gold revaluation dispute have increased the chances of a delay.
